title: Personal Finance and Budgeting
summary: Learn to track income and spending, build a monthly budget, start emergency savings and understand interest and the real cost of loans. Includes inflation, scam awareness and record keeping.
audience: Students and young adults who want to manage their own money

body.p: Personal finance means managing the money that comes to you and goes out from you. Income is money you receive: pocket money, wages, business profit, allowances, gifts, scholarships. Expenses are money you spend. If income is bigger than expenses you have a surplus you can save. If expenses are bigger you have a deficit, and the gap is filled by borrowing, using up savings, or going without.

Needs are things you must have to live and work or study: safe housing, basic food, transport to school or work, school fees and essential medicine. Wants are things that make life nicer but you could delay or do without: a new phone model, takeaway meals, extra clothes, entertainment. Some items sit in between. Data for study is a need; data for endless video is a want. A cheap meal is a need; a restaurant meal is a want. Be honest and decide for yourself.

body.h: Worked example: one month for a student (money units)

body.code:
Income: 85,000
rent share        30,000
food              22,000
transport          9,000
phone and data     4,000
school items       5,000
entertainment      6,000
Total expenses     76,000
Surplus = 85,000 - 76,000 = 9,000

body.p: Expenses are 89.4% of income, and the remaining 9,000 can be saved. Seeing the numbers on one page is often a surprise: small items such as snacks and airtime add up.

If you have a job, gross pay is the amount before deductions and net pay is what actually reaches you after deductions such as tax or pension contributions. Always plan with net pay, the money you can really spend. Deduction rules differ by country, so check your own payslip and your country's rules.

body.tip: For one week write down everything you spend, even small amounts. Most people find at least one habit they did not know was costing them.

body.p: Irregular income is common for traders, farmers and casual workers. In that case look at your last six months, find a low month, and base your budget on that smaller figure.

A budget is a plan for your money before the month begins. It does not stop you enjoying life. It makes sure that the important things are paid first and that you decide where your money goes instead of wondering where it went.

steps: List your expected net income for the month, using the lowest sensible figure.
List fixed needs first: rent, fees, transport, food, airtime and data.
Add savings as a bill you pay to yourself, early in the month.
Share what is left among wants.
At the end of the month compare plan and reality, and adjust the next budget.

body.p: Some people divide net income into 50% needs, 30% wants and 20% savings or debt repayment. With a monthly income of 120,000: needs 60,000, wants 36,000, savings 24,000. The three amounts add up to 120,000, which is the whole income.

This is a starting point, not a rule. If rent and food already cost 70% of your income, then 50% for needs is impossible, and a plan with needs at 70%, wants at 15% and savings at 15% may be more honest. For the student in lesson one, earning 85,000, needs of 70,000 are 82.4% of income, so that student would adapt the method to their own numbers.

list: Pay yourself first: move savings out as soon as money arrives.
Use envelopes or separate mobile wallets for food, transport and fun money.
Keep a small buffer line for surprises such as a repair or a family event.
Review every week for the first three months, then monthly.

body.tip: If your budget never balances, do not give up. Cut or delay the wants, look for extra income, or reduce a need by a cheaper choice, such as sharing transport.

body.p: Budgeting is a skill. The first budget is nearly always wrong, and that is fine. The second one is better because you now have real figures.

An emergency fund is money set aside for surprises: a sudden medical cost, a broken phone you need for work, a lost job, a family emergency. Without it, people often borrow at high cost in a hurry. With it, a problem stays a problem and does not become a debt trap.

A common starting guide is enough to cover essential expenses (needs only) for three to six months, but begin smaller. A first goal of one month of needs is already a strong shield. Your target depends on how steady your income is, how many people depend on you, and how easy it is to get help.

Essential monthly spending is 45,000. A three-month fund is 3 x 45,000 = 135,000. If you can save 9,000 a month, it will take 135,000 / 9,000 = 15 months. A first goal of one month, 45,000, takes 45,000 / 9,000 = 5.0 months, about 5 months.

list: Keep it separate from spending money, in a safe place that is easy to reach but not too tempting.
Use it only for real emergencies. A sale on shoes is not one.
If you use it, refill it before you increase wants.
Keep it safe and accessible. Use trusted, regulated providers where possible, and check what your country offers.

body.tip: Automate if you can: a small fixed amount moved on payday is easier than trying to save what is left at the end.

body.p: Start with whatever you can. Even a small amount each week builds the habit, and the habit matters more than the first figure.

Interest is the price of using money. When you save, the bank or provider may pay you interest. When you borrow, you pay interest to the lender. The rate is usually written as a percentage per period, most often per year. The rates in this course are examples to practise with, not real rates. Check current rates from your own providers.
Simple interest is calculated only on the original amount (the principal). Formula: interest = principal x rate x years.
Example: save 10,000 at 8% a year. Interest each year = 10,000 x 0.08 = 800. After 3 years simple interest is 2,400, and the total is 12,400.
With compound interest, each period's interest is added to the balance, so the next interest is earned on a bigger amount. Formula: final amount = principal x (1 + rate) ^ years.

body.code:
Principal 10,000, rate 8% per year
Year 1: 10,000 x 1.08 = 10,800.00
Year 2: 10,800.00 x 1.08 = 11,664.00
Year 3: 11,664.00 x 1.08 = 12,597.12
Compound interest after 3 years = 2,597.12
Simple interest after 3 years   = 2,400.00

body.p: Compound growth gives 197.12 more than simple interest in only three years. The longer the time, the bigger the gap. The same effect works against you with debt: unpaid interest is added and then charged interest too.
Principal 20,000, rate 6% a year, 4 years. Simple interest = 20,000 x 0.06 x 4 = 4,800. Compound: 20,000 x 1.06^4 = 25,249.54, so interest is 5,249.54.

body.tip: Always ask how often interest is added (monthly, quarterly, yearly) and whether the quoted rate is per month or per year. A rate per month is far larger than the same number per year.

body.p: This lesson is about understanding, not about choosing where to put your money. Check the terms and risks of any account with a regulated provider before you use it.

lessons.title: The real cost of borrowing and mobile loan traps

body.p: Borrowing can be sensible, for example for study or equipment that raises your income, if you can repay comfortably. But the real cost is the total you repay minus what you received, including fees, not the cheerful headline on an advert. Before borrowing, ask: how much will I receive, how much will I repay in total, by when, and what happens if I am late?
You borrow 36,000 and repay 4,000 each month for 12 months. Total repaid = 4,000 x 12 = 48,000. The cost of the loan is 48,000 - 36,000 = 12,000, which is 33.3% of the amount borrowed.

A second example: borrow 100,000 at 2% per month for 12 months with equal payments. The monthly payment is about 9,455.96, the total repaid is about 113,471.52, and the cost is about 13,471.52. The rate is an example only. Ask your lender for the exact monthly amount and total.

Quick loans on phones are easy to get and can be very expensive. Example: borrow 8,000 and repay 9,200 after 30 days. The cost is 1,200, which is 15% for just one month. If this rate continued all year the yearly equivalent would be very large: 15% x 365 / 30 = about 182% a year in simple terms.

The trap gets worse if you roll the loan over. Borrow 8,000 at 15% per 30 days and renew four times without paying anything off, and you owe 8,000 x 1.15^4 = 13,992.05. That is 5,992.05 more than you borrowed.

list: Read the full terms before pressing accept, including fees and late charges.
Borrow only what the budget can repay from your next income.
Never borrow from one lender to pay another unless you have a plan.
Check that the lender is registered or regulated where you live.
Be careful about what permissions you give an app, such as access to contacts.

body.tip: If you cannot repay, contact the lender before the due date, ask for options and seek help from a consumer advice organisation. Silence makes things worse.

body.p: Inflation means prices rise over time, so each unit of money buys less. If prices rise and your money sits unchanged, you can buy fewer things. Rates differ by country and by year, and the numbers below are examples for practice.

Suppose a loaf costs 800 and prices rise 5% a year. After 2 years: 800 x 1.05 x 1.05 = 882. Another: 12,000 buys 20 items at 600 each. If the price rises 25% to 750, the same 12,000 buys 12,000 / 750 = 16 items. Your money did not shrink, but its power to buy did.

At 10% a year a price of 500 becomes 550 after one year, 605 after two and 665.5 after three. The lesson: keep an eye on your real spending power, and ask for pay rises or look for ways to earn that keep up with rising prices.

list: Promises of 'double your money' or fast, guaranteed returns with no risk.
Pressure to act today, or secrecy ('do not tell anyone').
Asking you to pay a fee first to release a loan, prize or job.
Asking for your PIN, password or one-time code. A genuine bank or mobile money agent will not ask for these.
Messages from unknown numbers or links that copy a real company's name.

body.p: If something sounds too good to be true, it almost certainly is. Stop, do not pay, and check with the real organisation using a phone number or website you found yourself. Report scams to your local authorities or provider.

Keep receipts, loan agreements, mobile money messages and a monthly summary. They help you spot leaks. For example, spending 350 a day on snacks for 26 days is 350 x 26 = 9,100 a month. They also protect you in disputes.

steps: Pick a place: a notebook, spreadsheet or folder on your phone.
Record each purchase on the day.
Once a month add up spending by category and compare with your budget.
Keep important papers for as long as your country's rules or the agreement require.

body.tip: Protect your phone with a lock code and never share OTP codes or PINs with anyone.

quiz.q: A student receives 85,000 in a month and spends rent share 30,000, food 22,000, transport 9,000, phone 4,000, school items 5,000 and entertainment 6,000. What is the surplus?
Using 50/30/20 as an example on a net monthly income of 120,000, how much goes to savings?
Which statement about the 50/30/20 method is the most sensible?
options: It is a legal rule everyone must follow
It only works for people earning a salary
It means wants must always equal exactly 30%
It is one example; change the shares to fit your costs and income

quiz.q: A student wants to build an emergency fund of three months of essential spending. Essentials are 45,000 a month and they can save 9,000 a month. How many months to reach the goal?
What is the simple interest on 20,000 at 6% a year for 4 years?
What is the total after 4 years if 20,000 earns 6% interest compounded yearly?
How much more interest does compounding earn than simple interest on 20,000 at 6% over 4 years?
You borrow 8,000 on a phone app and repay 9,200 after 30 days. What is the cost of the loan as a percentage of the amount borrowed for that month?
If the same loan (8,000 with 15% cost per 30 days) is rolled over four times with nothing paid off, about how much is owed?
You borrow 36,000 and repay 4,000 a month for 12 months. What is the total cost of borrowing (the extra beyond what you received)?
A price of 800 rises by 5% each year for two years. What is the price after two years?
You have 12,000. Items cost 600 each, then the price rises by 25%. How many items can you buy after the rise?
A message says: 'Pay a small fee today to release your approved loan. Do not tell anyone.' What is the best response?
options: Pay quickly before the offer ends
Send your PIN so they can check your account
Forward it to friends so they can pay too
Do not pay; verify through the lender's official contact that you found yourself

quiz.q: A person spends 350 each day on snacks for 26 days of a month. How much is that for the month?
A person with net income 90,000 plans 36,000 for wants. What share of income is that?
